W4220703499.c007.text: The truth about, and knowledge of, a free choice depends upon that actual choice (Grounding Principle).

W4220703499.c011.text: If God knows at T1 that S will choose B at T2, then S lacks open options and power, so the choice is not free.
W4220703499.c011.quote: Hasker holds that this attempt to solve the dilemma of freedom and divine foreknowledge fails. On his understanding of “free will”, if S chooses B at T2, and if it is true at T1 that “S chooses B at T2”—as it must be if God foreknows S’s choice or if we live in an isotemporal universe—then S’s choice cannot really be free.

W4220703499.c012.text: Hasker’s PEP7 shows that, given God’s knowledge, S cannot be in power to refrain from choosing B, so S is not free at T2.
W4220703499.c012.quote: Take ‘P’ to be ‘God knows at T1 that S chooses B at T2.’ That entails ‘Q’; ‘S chooses B at T2.’ Assuming P, it cannot be in anyone’s power, including S’s, to bring it about that P is false.

W4220703499.c013.text: It is difficult to locate the time at which S could exercise the power Hasker requires, undermining Hasker’s analysis.
W4220703499.c013.quote: I find it difficult to pinpoint the time at which S might actually exercise the sort of power Hasker has in mind—the power involved in his definition of free will, that is, to choose A or to refrain from choosing A (say by choosing B).

W4220703499.c014.text: Hasker's analysis makes S unfree at the moment he actually chooses.
W4220703499.c014.quote: On Hasker’s analysis, this seems to render S unfree at the time he actually chooses.

W4220703499.c015.text: Since no one can make P false or Q false, S lacks the power required for free will at the time of his choice.
W4220703499.c015.quote: Since it is not in anyone’s power to bring it about that P is false, it is not in anyone’s power to bring it about that Q is false, and S does not have the power required for free will at the time he makes his choice.

W4220703499.c016.text: The logical necessity that if S chooses B at T2 then S chooses B at T2 is harmless and compatible with freedom.
W4220703499.c016.quote: The consequent necessity at work here seems to me innocuous vis‑à‑vis free will because it is just a logical necessity traceable to S’s own choice—if S chooses B at T2, then it cannot fail to be the case that S chooses B at T2.

W4220703499.c017.text: Hasker fails to analyze free‑will power in terms of the agent’s strength.
W4220703499.c017.quote: But Hasker does not analyze the power of free will in terms of the agent’s strength.

W4220703499.c018.text: Free‑will power must include the possibility of choosing otherwise, which makes the actual choice render the alternative impossible in a way that conflicts with freedom.
W4220703499.c018.quote: The agent’s power must include the possibility of choosing otherwise, where “possible” entails that the actual choosing by the agent makes it impossible for him to choose otherwise—impossible in a way that conflicts with free will.

W4220703499.c019.text: At T1 S cannot choose between A and B because he cannot be choosing before he is choosing.
W4220703499.c019.quote: It is not possible for S to choose between A and B at T1, since S cannot be choosing before he is choosing.

W4220703499.c021.quote: Hasker’s explication of that power, and hence his understanding of free will, does not strike me as intuitive.

W4220703499.c022.text: Hasker’s PEPs entail that God’s knowledge conflicts with human freedom even when that knowledge depends on the agent’s free choice.
W4220703499.c022.quote: And they entail that God’s knowledge conflicts with human freedom, even if the knowledge is dependent on the agent’s free choice.

objections.text: Consider Maya, a chess player at T1 who is weighing two moves, A (Nf3) and B (d4). She deliberates for ten seconds, then plays A. Her premise is that she is choosing now, while the options are open. Suppose a rival says: 'At T1 you cannot choose between A and B, since choosing is something you can only be doing after you have chosen.' Test this against Maya's case. Her deliberation is itself the process of choosing: weighing reasons, rejecting B, settling on A. Nothing in that process requires the choice to be complete before it begins. If choosing could occur only after it had finished, no one could ever deliberate toward a decision, and Maya's ten seconds would be idle. The inference treats 'is choosing' as a state that must already hold, when for a free agent it is the activity that makes the choice occur. The claim that one cannot be choosing before one is choosing is true only if 'choosing' names a completed event, which begs the question about whether T1 is open.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c019 fails because it assumes that 'choosing' is a completed state that must already obtain before deliberation can count as choosing, whereas Maya's case shows that choosing is an ongoing activity that is open at T1 and can be in progress before its outcome is settled.

objections.text: Ann knows on Tuesday that Sam will freely choose pancakes Friday. She knows this because Sam told her his intention Tuesday, and over twenty years he has never changed his mind after such announcements, though he always could. Friday arrives and Sam freely chooses pancakes. Ann's knowledge on Tuesday did not depend on Friday's actual choice—which had not yet occurred—but on Sam's testimony and reliable pattern. Knowledge of a free choice here rests on pre-choice evidence rather than the actual choice.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4220703499.c007 fails because knowledge of a free choice can be grounded in pre-choice evidence such as testimony and track record rather than depending on the actual choice itself.

objections.text: Sarah faces a choice at T2: she can help a stranger or walk past. God is eternal, with all moments present to Him, so God perceives Sarah walking past at T2—not as a prediction but as a present, completed reality within His timeless awareness. God's eternal perception is fixed and unalterable; it encompasses the entire timeline as one undivided whole. Now Sarah at T2 deliberates. For libertarian freedom, it must be within Sarah's power to help instead. But if Sarah were to help, God's eternal perception would have included her helping—which it does not. Since God's perception is eternally complete and cannot be otherwise, Sarah cannot do otherwise than what God perceives. The fixity is not removed; it is made permanent. Compare open theism: God knows all real possibilities but not which choice Sarah will make, leaving her future genuinely open. This alternative better respects libertarian freedom, since Sarah's choice remains undetermined by any prior or eternal fact.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c025 fails because positing God as eternal with all time present to Him does not best respect libertarian free will: it merely relocates the fixity of Sarah's choice from temporal foreknowledge to timeless perception, leaving her unable to do otherwise than what God eternally apprehends.

objections.text: Agent S is deliberating at T about whether to raise her arm at T+1. She believes she is free to choose either way, and her choice is not determined by prior causes. However, it is necessarily true that if S will raise her arm at T+1, then she will raise her arm at T+1. This is a trivial internal necessity of the form 'If X then X'. Yet, if God knows at T that S will raise her arm at T+1, then S cannot do otherwise at T+1 without contradicting God’s infallible knowledge, thus undermining her libertarian freedom.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.c010 fails because even trivial internal necessities like 'If X then X' can conflict with free will when combined with divine foreknowledge.

objections.text: Maria is a surgeon who has settled, over twenty years of practice, that she will never abandon a patient mid-operation. A cardiac arrest occurs. No one coerces her, no drug impels her, no external cause determines her action. She continues the surgery. There was, in effect, only one live option: she could not, given her settled character, genuinely entertain abandonment as a live alternative. No external force closes that option; her own dispositions do. Yet her choice is fully aseity—grounded in herself, uncaused from outside, hers to execute. The premise insists aseity requires that options be open and that it be up to him which option he chooses, implying multiple live alternatives he genuinely picks among. But Maria's self-grounded act occurs with no open alternatives; it is still uncoerced, still her own, still aseity. The premise's condition is stronger than aseity requires.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.c006 fails because Maria's uncoerced, self-grounded choice with no open alternatives shows that aseity does not require facing multiple open options or picking among them; a settled character can act with full self-grounding from a single viable course.

objections.text: Consider a scenario where an eternal God exists, but human perception of time is relative and dynamic. In this case, a person, Alice, makes a choice that she believes is free, but God's eternal presence means that her choice is already known. However, Alice's understanding of her own freedom is rooted in her experience of time, which is not absolute. If we prioritize Alice's perspective, we see that her choice feels free to her, despite God's foreknowledge.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes an eternal God's perspective on time must align with human understanding of freedom, which is not necessarily the case.

objections.text: Consider Sarah, a rational agent at T1 who must choose between donating to charity A or B. In a Molinist framework God, outside time, knows the true counterfactuals: if Sarah were to freely choose A, then she would later be satisfied; if she were to freely choose B, she would regret it. God’s middle knowledge fixes the actual world by selecting the counterfactual where Sarah freely chooses A, but this does not require that God sees a static, eternal present of the whole timeline. If instead we posit God’s eternity as a timeless present where the entire history, including Sarah’s choice, is already laid out, Sarah’s decision is no longer open to her; it is simply a point on God’s already‑present timeline, contradicting the Molinist claim that libertarian freedom is preserved by counterfactuals, not by a static eternal view.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4220703499.c025 fails because Molinism holds that God’s middle knowledge, not an eternal present, secures libertarian freedom, and the eternal‑present view makes choices non‑open.

objections.text: Imagine a man named Elias who chooses to drink water at noon. According to the Grounding Principle, the truth of this choice and the knowledge of it are grounded in Elias's act. If God's knowledge of Elias's choice depends on that contingent act, then God's knowledge is not identical to His necessary essence. Since God is absolutely simple, His knowledge is His being. If His knowledge is grounded in a creature's choice, then God's very existence becomes contingent upon the world, violating divine simplicity and aseity.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.c007 fails because grounding divine knowledge in contingent creaturely acts contradicts divine simplicity and the necessity of God's essence.

objections.text: Suppose an agent, Clara, is deciding at T1 whether to accept or reject a gift at T2. Because God is eternal and perceives the entire timeline at once, the fact that Clara accepts the gift at T2 is eternally present to Him. Since this fact is eternally true, Clara cannot choose to reject the gift at T2, as doing so would contradict the eternal reality God perceives. Consequently, Clara lacks the open options necessary for libertarian freedom.
objections.premise_fails_because: The eternal fixedness of the timeline precludes the existence of open options, meaning the theory fails to respect libertarian freedom.

objections.text: Consider Maren, a creature who at noon on Tuesday freely decides to keep a promise rather than break it. God, eternally present to all time, knows at dawn that Maren will keep it. Suppose God's knowing at dawn is grounded in nothing creaturely: it is wholly self-originating. Now ask what it is for that knowing to be the knowing that Maren keeps the promise. Its object is fixed by a fact that holds only because Maren's noon decision occurs. If the object is grounded in her act while the knowing is not, then the knowing is correct without being answerable to anything in the world, and it would be correct even had Maren broken the promise, provided the object had been different. So the knowing's content varies with her act while the knowing does not, which means it is a knowing of nothing in particular: a dispositional state that happens to be co-extensive with Maren's act. The premise stipulates an asymmetry that cannot be stated as knowledge at all.
objections.premise_fails_because: r1 assumes God's knowing can be ungrounded in creaturely acts while its propositional objects are grounded in them, but a knowing whose correctness and content covary with the act cannot be ungrounded in that act, so the asymmetry collapses.

objections.text: Consider an eternal being, Alpha, for whom all times are present. At the eternal now, Jones's choice of cake over pie is fully present. Alpha's mind, however, hosts a timeless internal mirror that automatically duplicates every temporal event. Alpha's conscious state tracks this duplicate, not the act itself. If the duplicate were generated by a glitch while the act failed to occur, Alpha would still register "Jones chooses cake." Thus Alpha's state is merely a correlated disposition toward the duplicate. The actual choice is eternally present, but presence alone does not make Alpha's cognition answerable to the real act; it remains answerable to the internal copy. Therefore, eternal presence does not suffice to establish that knowledge of a temporal act is knowledge of the act itself rather than a correlated disposition.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.arg1.r2 fails because the mere eternal presence of a temporal act to a mind does not prevent that mind's state from being a correlated disposition toward an internal duplicate rather than direct knowledge of the act itself.

objections.text: Professor Chen posits an eternal God with all time present to Him. This respects divine foreknowledge: God timelessly knows S's choice at T2. It respects libertarian freedom: God's eternal awareness doesn't causally determine S's choice—S deliberates and decides autonomously. Yet reconciliation fails given this very theory of time. If all moments are equally real and present to God, S's future choice at T2 is as fixed as any past event. At T1, S faces no genuinely open alternatives: his choosing A at T2 is an unchangeable feature of the eternal landscape, just as Caesar's crossing the Rubicon is settled. The eternalist theory of time that supports God's timeless knowledge simultaneously eliminates the open future libertarian freedom requires.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4220703499.arg1.r3 fails because 'respecting' libertarian freedom (not causally determining the choice) is insufficient for reconciliation when the eternalist theory of time that the premise invokes fixes the future and removes the open alternatives libertarian freedom requires.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection attacks W4220703499.c007 as stated. The Grounding Principle claims that 'knowledge of a free choice depends upon that actual choice' without restricting whose knowledge is at issue. The objection takes this at face value, applies it to God's knowledge, and argues that the resulting dependency creates theological problems for divine simplicity and aseity. Whether or not this objection succeeds, it engages the premise as written rather than attacking a version the argument does not assert.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: The objection equivocates between two dependence claims. c007 concerns the truth of propositions about Elias's choice and the knowledge of them, i.e. that the proposition 'Elias drinks at noon' is true and known because he drinks. It is a claim about the relation between a contingent act and a truth-value/epistemic state, not a claim that God's cognitive act is caused by or grounded in the creature. Whether the 'knowledge' in question is a relation to a contingent proposition (a Cambridge-style or extrinsic feature) or an intrinsic state of God is exactly what the eternalist framework is designed to separate. On the view the argument supports, God's knowing is eternal and simple; the relational truth that He knows Elias's choice is what varies with the choice, as with any extrinsic predicate. That is consistent with simplicity, which governs intrinsic identity, not every true relational predication. Compare the Molinist distinction in [W4246671415.a3], where God's middle knowledge concerns counterfactuals not grounded in God, and [W7202131248.a3], where God's knowledge of Pilate's act is not future to God and so does not constitute its coercion. Neither implies that God's essence depends on the act. Still, the objection exposes a real cost: if the Grounding Principle is read as making God's knowledge itself grounded in creaturely acts, aseity is threatened. So the argument must restrict c007 to propositional truth and knowledge-of-the-proposition, and say that God's intrinsic knowing is ungrounded. That restriction is needed, and I accept it.
rounds.revised_premise: The Grounding Principle applies only to the truth of propositions about a free choice and to extrinsic knowledge-of-those-propositions, not to God's intrinsic knowing, which is ungrounded in creatures.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You attempt to preserve simplicity by distinguishing between God’s intrinsic cognitive state and the extrinsic truth of His knowing. However, this does not resolve the tension. If the truth of the proposition "God knows X" is grounded in a contingent act, then a truth-value concerning God’s omniscience is contingent upon the creature. For an eternal, simple being, if the truth of His knowing varies, then the reality of His omniscience is not an immutable aspect of His essence, but is dependent on temporal contingencies, violating aseity. 

Furthermore, by restricting c007 so that it no longer applies to God's actual knowledge, you have abandoned the very grounding mechanism intended to bridge the gap between choice and foreknowledge. You have preserved simplicity only by sacrificing the principle that was supposed to make the reconciliation possible.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Your rejoinder rightly presses the extrinsic/intrinsic line, but it does not show that the argument fails. Grant that 'God knows that Elias drinks' is true because Elias drinks. That makes a relational truth about God vary with the creature, but aseity and simplicity have never required that every true predication about God be non-relational; they concern what God is. God's essence, His eternal knowing, and His omniscience as an immutable perfection are unchanged, since the truth-maker of the relational predication is the creature's act, not any change in God. This is the structure the eternalist framework intends, and it is what [W4220703499.c025] is meant to secure: with all time present to God, God's knowing of Elias's act is not a temporally prior state that the act could alter. On your second point, I do not abandon the grounding mechanism. c007 still does its work for propositional truth and for knowledge-of-the-proposition, which is what the reconciliation needs: the truth that the choice will be made is settled by the choice, and God's eternal knowing has that truth as its object. The bridge is therefore kept, but restricted to the object-side of divine knowledge. Where I concede: if c007 must also ground God's intrinsic knowing, the argument fails, and the premise needed is that God's knowing is ungrounded in creaturely acts while its objects are grounded in them.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the asymmetry is the crux, but you move too fast from 'ungrounded in creaturely acts' to 'answerable to nothing.' The grounding principle [W4220703499.c007] is an asymmetry of dependence, not of relation. God's knowing is correct because its object is the case; it is not correct because the object was made to be the case by the knowing. Correctness is a relation between the knowing and a fact that the fact fixes, and the fact fixing the knowing's correctness is exactly what the argument asserts. So the knowing is answerable to the world in the only sense that matters for knowledge: it would be false if the object were different. Your counterfactual (it would be correct had Maren broken the promise, 'provided the object had been different') is accurate, and it shows the knowing is modally sensitive to its object, which is what knowledge requires. What it does not show is that the knowing must itself be grounded in the act. The argument's claim that God's eternal presence to all time lets the knowing be non-derivative [W4220703499.c025] is consistent with that sensitivity. The 'knowing of nothing in particular' charge needs the further premise that a knowing is a knowing only if its determinate content is fixed by something upstream of it. The argument denies that premise for God, and it is not obvious the denial is incoherent. I concede the reply is only as strong as the claim that eternal presence does not make the knowing a mere disposition, and that claim needs defence the argument does not yet supply. The argument survives this objection without change, but only as a defence of asymmetric dependence, not as a defence of mutual answerability.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
Your reply concedes too much to the wrong target. My objection never needed the claim that the knowing must be grounded in the act. It needed only that the knowing's determinate content is fixed by the act, and you grant that. Your sensitivity point, that the knowing "would be false if the object were different," is exactly the modal profile I described, and it shows the knowing has a content that varies with Maren's noon decision while the knowing itself does not. That is the situation I called a disposition co-extensive with her act.

You say the charge needs a further premise, that a knowing is a knowing only if its content is fixed upstream. I do not need that premise in general. I need only the weaker one that a state whose content is wholly determined by a fact it does not depend on, and which could not have differed had that fact differed, is not yet shown to be a knowing of that fact rather than a state that tracks it. Your reply does not supply the missing link. Sensitivity of content to object is not the same as answerability of the knowing to the object, and you have just defended the first while the premise needs the second.

So I press the question you left open: what in eternal presence makes the knowing of Maren's noon act rather than merely correlated with it? Until that is answered, the asymmetry remains unstated as knowledge.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that my earlier reply conflated sensitivity of content with answerability of the knowing, and I accept that distinction. But the rejoinder still asks for something the argument does not claim to supply. The argument's claim is that God's knowing is ungrounded in creaturely acts while its objects are grounded in them [W4220703499.arg1.r1], and that eternal presence to all time lets God's knowing be of the temporal act rather than of a prior surrogate [W4220703499.c025]. What makes the knowing of Maren's noon act rather than merely correlated with it is that the knowing is of that act as present to God, and nothing in the modal profile separates 'tracking a fact' from 'knowing it' when the fact is present to the knower; the asymmetry concerns the direction of dependence, not the existence of a relation. The objector's test (a state whose content varies with the fact while the state does not depend on it is not yet a knowing) is a further premise, and I concede the argument does not supply a defence of it. The remark that it is a mistake to say anything is logically prior to God's whole act [W4220703499.c038] supports the denial of upstream determination but does not show the knowing is of the act and not of a correlate. So the argument survives only if eternal presence is itself the relation that makes tracking a knowing, and that identification is the premise the argument needs but does not state.

Revised premise: God's knowing of a temporal act is knowledge of that act, rather than a correlated disposition, because the act is eternally present to God, so that presence itself is the answerability relation between knowing and object.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: The mirror case is a good test, but it builds in a premise r2 does not state: that Alpha's cognition has the duplicate as its immediate object. r2 says God's knowing of a temporal act is knowledge of that act because the act is eternally present to God, and that presence is itself the answerability relation. On that reading, a glitch-generated duplicate with no act behind it is not an eternally present object at all, so the case is not one where presence holds and answerability fails. The objection's counterfactual ("if the duplicate were generated by a glitch while the act failed to occur") also changes the case: it removes the act while keeping the knowing, which is exactly what r2 denies can happen for an eternally present act. Still, the objection exposes a real gap. Presence must be shown to be a relation that fixes the object of knowing rather than merely co-occurring with it, and r2 as stated does not do that. The grounding principle [W4220703499.c007] helps only for the creaturely side, and the claim that it is logically prior or subsequent within God's act [W4220703499.c027] is contested, since it may be a mistake to locate anything prior or subsequent to God's whole act [W4220703499.c038]. So I defend the argument against this specific counterexample but not against the demand for a non-question-begging account of presence-as-answerability.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You concede the very issue: your premise does not show that presence fixes the object of knowing rather than merely co-occurring with it. Your reply blocks the mirror case only by insisting that God's knowing and the act cannot come apart, but that is the circularity the objection targets. If eternal presence guaranteed that the act itself is the object, the glitch scenario would indeed be impossible; yet your premise gives no non-question-begging reason why presence is object-constituting rather than representational. By conceding the gap remains, you admit the argument lacks the needed bridge from co-presence to answerability. Unless presence is independently shown to be the relation itself—and not just a correlated disposition wearing the label "presence"—the specific conclusion fails. I therefore withdraw the mirror as a purported counterexample, but press the deeper point: your premise assumes the compatibility it claims to establish.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that my last reply left a gap, and I will not paper over it. But your rejoinder runs two claims together. First, the mirror case is not a counterexample to r2 as stated: r2 makes the act itself the object of God's knowing because it is eternally present, and a glitch duplicate with no act is not present to God in that sense, so the counterfactual changes the case rather than testing it. Second, you are right that presence must be shown to fix the object rather than merely co-occur with it, and that this cannot be shown by insisting that knowing and act cannot come apart. The circularity charge is fair against that insistence. What r2 needs is an independent characterization of presence as a relation of acquaintance with the act's own temporal location in the eternal now, not a representational state that could be satisfied by a surrogate. The literature gives me no such characterization. The grounding principle [W4220703499.c007] settles only the creaturely direction, and the claim that God's act has a logical order [W4220703499.c027] is contested by [W4220703499.c038]. So the argument as stated does not survive: r2 assumes the compatibility it was meant to establish. I concede that.

Revised premise: Divine knowledge of a temporal act is knowledge of that act itself, not of a representational surrogate, because the eternal presence of the act to God is an acquaintance relation that is independently characterized as object-fixing, not merely co-occurring with the act.

The objection argues that this very view makes Sarah's decision no longer open to her, thereby undermining libertarian freedom. This is a direct attack on the premise as stated, not an attack on a different claim or a stronger/weaker version of it.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: The objection's central inference is that if Sarah's choice is already a point on God's present timeline, it is no longer open to her. That inference needs a premise the argument rejects: that what is present to God is settled prior to, and independently of, Sarah's deliberation. The Grounding Principle (c007) denies this. The truth about the choice depends on the actual choice, so the eternal presence is presence of an act that is being made, not a prior fixing that makes the act unfree. The Boethian point that God sees all time as present, and that this imposes no necessity conflicting with freedom [W4398759601.a1], is the relevant grounding. Likewise, what is future to Pilate is not future to God, so God's knowledge does not coerce the act [W7202135789.a3]. Where the objection says the present is 'already laid out', the argument can reply that a logical priority within God's eternal act, not a temporal prior, is what matters [W4220703499.c027]. The objection is right that the argument owes an account of how eternal presence avoids settling the act. Grounding supplies one, but it is not yet developed, and the mp premise connecting eternity to reconciliation remains unstated. I do not concede, since the objection does not show that presence entails settledness without the rival premise that the grounding principle denies. I do note that this is where the argument is thinnest.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: Defender, you concede that the argument “owes an account of how eternal presence avoids settling the act” and then invoke the Grounding Principle as if it already supplies that account. But you have not shown *why* a timelessly present act can be ontologically open. To claim that God’s knowledge is “logically prior” merely restates the premise you need; it does not demonstrate that the presentness of the act does not imply a settled truth‑value. Without an explicit mechanism—e.g., a coherent account of a truth‑maker that is both present to God and yet indeterminate for the agent—the objection that Sarah’s choice is fixed remains unanswered. Thus the reply circles back to an unproved premise, and the objection still forces the argument to explain how God’s eternal view coexists with genuine libertarian openness.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that my earlier reply leaned on the Grounding Principle without showing the mechanism, and I accept that the rejoinder exposes a gap. But the gap is narrower than 'the presentness implies settledness.' Your inference needs the premise that a truth about an act is settled whenever the act is present to a knower. The argument denies that premise: under c007, the truth-value of Sarah's choice is grounded in the choice she actually makes, so what is eternally present to God is the actual choice, and the truth about it is answerable to it rather than prior to it. Boethius makes the same structural move, that seeing all time as present imposes no necessity on freedom [W4398759601.a1], and the Pilate literature makes it sharper: what is future to Pilate is not future to God, so God's knowledge does not coerce the act [W7202135789.a3]. The truth-maker is the act itself, which is open to Sarah because nothing upstream of her deliberation fixes it. Your demand for a truth-maker 'both present to God and indeterminate for the agent' is answered by saying the act is indeterminate for her until she makes it, and present to God as made. Whether that is coherent is the real dispute, and it is not settled by the objection alone. I therefore do not concede the objection as stated. I do concede that the argument currently lacks a developed account of how eternal presence and the grounding relation fit together, and that the unstated mp premise must be made explicit.

Instead, it claims that God’s knowing of a temporal act is knowledge of that act because the act is eternally present to God, and this presence itself constitutes the answerability relation between knowing and object [W4220703499.arg1.r2]. Because what remains future to Sarah is not future to God, his eternal knowledge does not coerce her temporal act [W7202135789.a3, W7202149095.a3]. The grounding principle ensures that the truth about her choice depends upon her actual choice, so God’s eternal knowledge does not render the future fixed prior to her decision [W4220703499.c007]. Moreover, it makes sense to speak of logical priority and succession within God’s eternal act, so Sarah’s choice remains open from her temporal standpoint even as God knows it eternally [W4220703499.c027]. Libertarian freedom is preserved not by counterfactuals but by the asymmetry between eternal and temporal perspectives.

Thus the future is already fixed, not merely known. Unless you concede that God’s “knowledge of the act” is really a disposition toward a future event, the claim that Sarah’s options remain open is unsubstantiated. Either revise premise r2 to deny eternal presence as knowledge of the act, or accept that the argument fails to reconcile libertarian freedom with such a God. As it stands, your reply does not save the thesis.

An internal necessity of the form 'If X then X' does not conflict with free will [W4220703499.c010], so the fact that God eternally knows what she freely does does not impose a determinative necessity on her act. Because God's knowing is ungrounded in creaturely acts while its objects are grounded in them [W4220703499.arg1.r1], the eternal presence of the act is not a pre-existing fact that renders her choice necessary; it is the presence of the very act she contributes freely. Therefore eternal presence does not collapse into fixity, and r2 stands. The argument survives.

objection.text: Consider Maya, a chess player at T1 who is weighing two moves, A (Nf3) and B (d4). She deliberates for ten seconds, then plays A. Her premise is that she is choosing now, while the options are open. Suppose a rival says: 'At T1 you cannot choose between A and B, since choosing is something you can only be doing after you have chosen.' Test this against Maya's case. Her deliberation is itself the process of choosing: weighing reasons, rejecting B, settling on A. Nothing in that process requires the choice to be complete before it begins. If choosing could occur only after it had finished, no one could ever deliberate toward a decision, and Maya's ten seconds would be idle. The inference treats 'is choosing' as a state that must already hold, when for a free agent it is the activity that makes the choice occur. The claim that one cannot be choosing before one is choosing is true only if 'choosing' names a completed event, which begs the question about whether T1 is open.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c019 fails because it assumes that 'choosing' is a completed state that must already obtain before deliberation can count as choosing, whereas Maya's case shows that choosing is an ongoing activity that is open at T1 and can be in progress before its outcome is settled.

objection.text: Ann knows on Tuesday that Sam will freely choose pancakes Friday. She knows this because Sam told her his intention Tuesday, and over twenty years he has never changed his mind after such announcements, though he always could. Knowledge of a free choice here rests on pre-choice evidence rather than the actual choice.

objection.text: Sarah faces a choice at T2: she can help a stranger or walk past. God is eternal, with all moments present to Him, so God perceives Sarah walking past at T2—not as a prediction but as a present, completed reality within His timeless awareness. God's eternal perception is fixed and unalterable; it encompasses the entire timeline as one undivided whole. Now Sarah at T2 deliberates. For libertarian freedom, it must be within Sarah's power to help instead. But if Sarah were to help, God's eternal perception would have included her helping—which it does not. Since God's perception is eternally complete and cannot be otherwise, Sarah cannot do otherwise than what God perceives. The fixity is not removed; it is made permanent. Compare open theism: God knows all real possibilities but not which choice Sarah will make, leaving her future genuinely open. This alternative better respects libertarian freedom, since Sarah's choice remains undetermined by any prior or eternal fact.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c025 fails because positing God as eternal with all time present to Him does not best respect libertarian free will: it merely relocates the fixity of Sarah's choice from temporal foreknowledge to timeless perception, leaving her unable to do otherwise than what God eternally apprehends.

objection.text: Agent S is deliberating at T about whether to raise her arm at T+1. She believes she is free to choose either way, and her choice is not determined by prior causes. Yet, if God knows at T that S will raise her arm at T+1, then S cannot do otherwise at T+1 without contradicting God’s infallible knowledge, thus undermining her libertarian freedom.
objection.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.c010 fails because even trivial internal necessities like 'If X then X' can conflict with free will when combined with divine foreknowledge.

objection.text: Maria is a surgeon who has settled, over twenty years of practice, that she will never abandon a patient mid-operation. A cardiac arrest occurs. No one coerces her, no drug impels her, no external cause determines her action. She continues the surgery. There was, in effect, only one live option: she could not, given her settled character, genuinely entertain abandonment as a live alternative. No external force closes that option; her own dispositions do. Yet her choice is fully aseity—grounded in herself, uncaused from outside, hers to execute. The premise insists aseity requires that options be open and that it be up to him which option he chooses, implying multiple live alternatives he genuinely picks among. But Maria's self-grounded act occurs with no open alternatives; it is still uncoerced, still her own, still aseity. The premise's condition is stronger than aseity requires.
objection.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.c006 fails because Maria's uncoerced, self-grounded choice with no open alternatives shows that aseity does not require facing multiple open options or picking among them; a settled character can act with full self-grounding from a single viable course.

objection.text: Consider a scenario where an eternal God exists, but human perception of time is relative and dynamic. objection.text: Consider Sarah, a rational agent at T1 who must choose between donating to charity A or B. In a Molinist framework God, outside time, knows the true counterfactuals: if Sarah were to freely choose A, then she would later be satisfied; if she were to freely choose B, she would regret it. God’s middle knowledge fixes the actual world by selecting the counterfactual where Sarah freely chooses A, but this does not require that God sees a static, eternal present of the whole timeline. If instead we posit God’s eternity as a timeless present where the entire history, including Sarah’s choice, is already laid out, Sarah’s decision is no longer open to her; it is simply a point on God’s already‑present timeline, contradicting the Molinist claim that libertarian freedom is preserved by counterfactuals, not by a static eternal view.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W4220703499.c025 fails because Molinism holds that God’s middle knowledge, not an eternal present, secures libertarian freedom, and the eternal‑present view makes choices non‑open.

objection.text: Imagine a man named Elias who chooses to drink water at noon. According to the Grounding Principle, the truth of this choice and the knowledge of it are grounded in Elias's act. If His knowledge is grounded in a creature's choice, then God's very existence becomes contingent upon the world, violating divine simplicity and aseity.
objection.premise_fails_because: W4220703499.c007 fails because grounding divine knowledge in contingent creaturely acts contradicts divine simplicity and the necessity of God's essence.

objection.text: Suppose an agent, Clara, is deciding at T1 whether to accept or reject a gift at T2. turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: The objection equivocates between two dependence claims. c007 concerns the truth of propositions about Elias's choice and the knowledge of them, i.e. that the proposition 'Elias drinks at noon' is true and known because he drinks. It is a claim about the relation between a contingent act and a truth-value/epistemic state, not a claim that God's cognitive act is caused by or grounded in the creature. Whether the 'knowledge' in question is a relation to a contingent proposition (a Cambridge-style or extrinsic feature) or an intrinsic state of God is exactly what the eternalist framework is designed to separate. On the view the argument supports, God's knowing is eternal and simple; the relational truth that He knows Elias's choice is what varies with the choice, as with any extrinsic predicate. That is consistent with simplicity, which governs intrinsic identity, not every true relational predication. Compare the Molinist distinction in [W4246671415.a3], where God's middle knowledge concerns counterfactuals not grounded in God, and [W7202131248.a3], where God's knowledge of Pilate's act is not future to God and so does not constitute its coercion. Neither implies that God's essence depends on the act. Still, the objection exposes a real cost: if the Grounding Principle is read as making God's knowledge itself grounded in creaturely acts, aseity is threatened. So the argument must restrict c007 to propositional truth and knowledge-of-the-proposition, and say that God's intrinsic knowing is ungrounded. That restriction is needed, and I accept it.

turn.content:
You attempt to preserve simplicity by distinguishing between God’s intrinsic cognitive state and the extrinsic truth of His knowing. However, this does not resolve the tension. If the truth of the proposition "God knows X" is grounded in a contingent act, then a truth-value concerning God’s omniscience is contingent upon the creature. For an eternal, simple being, if the truth of His knowing varies, then the reality of His omniscience is not an immutable aspect of His essence, but is dependent on temporal contingencies, violating aseity. 

Furthermore, by restricting c007 so that it no longer applies to God's actual knowledge, you have abandoned the very grounding mechanism intended to bridge the gap between choice and foreknowledge. You have preserved simplicity only by sacrificing the principle that was supposed to make the reconciliation possible.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: Your rejoinder rightly presses the extrinsic/intrinsic line, but it does not show that the argument fails. Grant that 'God knows that Elias drinks' is true because Elias drinks. That makes a relational truth about God vary with the creature, but aseity and simplicity have never required that every true predication about God be non-relational; they concern what God is. God's essence, His eternal knowing, and His omniscience as an immutable perfection are unchanged, since the truth-maker of the relational predication is the creature's act, not any change in God. This is the structure the eternalist framework intends, and it is what [W4220703499.c025] is meant to secure: with all time present to God, God's knowing of Elias's act is not a temporally prior state that the act could alter. On your second point, I do not abandon the grounding mechanism. c007 still does its work for propositional truth and for knowledge-of-the-proposition, which is what the reconciliation needs: the truth that the choice will be made is settled by the choice, and God's eternal knowing has that truth as its object. The bridge is therefore kept, but restricted to the object-side of divine knowledge. Where I concede: if c007 must also ground God's intrinsic knowing, the argument fails, and the premise needed is that God's knowing is ungrounded in creaturely acts while its objects are grounded in them.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
You are right that if the Grounding Principle meant God's act of knowing were caused or sustained by Elias's choice, divine simplicity would be imperiled. But the argument does not claim that. It claims only that the truth of the proposition about Elias's choice is grounded in his act [W4220703499.c007]. Because God is eternal and all time is present to Him [W4220703499.c025], God eternally knows every true proposition without temporal posteriority or causal dependence on the creature; what is future to Elias is not future to God [W7202131248.a3]. The creature determines which proposition is true, not whether God knows it. Still, your worry exposes a genuine ambiguity: the argument must explicitly rule out any reading on which contingent content enters into the constitution of the divine essence. That requires an added premise.

Revised premise: The Grounding Principle grounds only the truth of the contingent proposition in the agent's free choice, while God's eternal knowledge of that truth is a necessary extrinsic relation that does not enter into the constitution of His simple essence.

objection.text: Consider Maren, a creature who at noon on Tuesday freely decides to keep a promise rather than break it. God, eternally present to all time, knows at dawn that Maren will keep it. Suppose God's knowing at dawn is grounded in nothing creaturely: it is wholly self-originating. Now ask what it is for that knowing to be the knowing that Maren keeps the promise. Its object is fixed by a fact that holds only because Maren's noon decision occurs. If the object is grounded in her act while the knowing is not, then the knowing is correct without being answerable to anything in the world, and it would be correct even had Maren broken the promise, provided the object had been different. So the knowing's content varies with her act while the knowing does not, which means it is a knowing of nothing in particular: a dispositional state that happens to be co-extensive with Maren's act. The premise stipulates an asymmetry that cannot be stated as knowledge at all.
objection.premise_fails_because: r1 assumes God's knowing can be ungrounded in creaturely acts while its propositional objects are grounded in them, but a knowing whose correctness and content covary with the act cannot be ungrounded in that act, so the asymmetry collapses.

The premise claims that God's knowing is ungrounded in creaturely acts while its objects are grounded in them. The objection engages precisely with this asymmetry and argues it is incoherent—that such a knowing cannot count as knowledge at all. This is an attack on the premise as stated, not on a stronger or weaker version or a different claim.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: You are right that the asymmetry is the crux, but you move too fast from 'ungrounded in creaturely acts' to 'answerable to nothing.' The grounding principle [W4220703499.c007] is an asymmetry of dependence, not of relation. God's knowing is correct because its object is the case; it is not correct because the object was made to be the case by the knowing. Correctness is a relation between the knowing and a fact that the fact fixes, and the fact fixing the knowing's correctness is exactly what the argument asserts. So the knowing is answerable to the world in the only sense that matters for knowledge: it would be false if the object were different. Your counterfactual (it would be correct had Maren broken the promise, 'provided the object had been different') is accurate, and it shows the knowing is modally sensitive to its object, which is what knowledge requires. What it does not show is that the knowing must itself be grounded in the act. The argument's claim that God's eternal presence to all time lets the knowing be non-derivative [W4220703499.c025] is consistent with that sensitivity. The 'knowing of nothing in particular' charge needs the further premise that a knowing is a knowing only if its determinate content is fixed by something upstream of it. The argument denies that premise for God, and it is not obvious the denial is incoherent. I concede the reply is only as strong as the claim that eternal presence does not make the knowing a mere disposition, and that claim needs defence the argument does not yet supply. The argument survives this objection without change, but only as a defence of asymmetric dependence, not as a defence of mutual answerability.

This attacks a phenomenological claim about the experience of freedom, not the metaphysical claim about libertarian freedom that the premise actually makes. The argument never claims that choices merely feel free; it claims they are free in the libertarian sense.

Your reply concedes too much to the wrong target. My objection never needed the claim that the knowing must be grounded in the act. It needed only that the knowing's determinate content is fixed by the act, and you grant that. Your sensitivity point, that the knowing "would be false if the object were different," is exactly the modal profile I described, and it shows the knowing has a content that varies with Maren's noon decision while the knowing itself does not. That is the situation I called a disposition co-extensive with her act.

You say the charge needs a further premise, that a knowing is a knowing only if its content is fixed upstream. I do not need that premise in general. I need only the weaker one that a state whose content is wholly determined by a fact it does not depend on, and which could not have differed had that fact differed, is not yet shown to be a knowing of that fact rather than a state that tracks it. Your reply does not supply the missing link. Sensitivity of content to object is not the same as answerability of the knowing to the object, and you have just defended the first while the premise needs the second.

So I press the question you left open: what in eternal presence makes the knowing of Maren's noon act rather than merely correlated with it? Until that is answered, the asymmetry remains unstated as knowledge.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that my earlier reply conflated sensitivity of content with answerability of the knowing, and I accept that distinction. But the rejoinder still asks for something the argument does not claim to supply. The argument's claim is that God's knowing is ungrounded in creaturely acts while its objects are grounded in them [W4220703499.arg1.r1], and that eternal presence to all time lets God's knowing be of the temporal act rather than of a prior surrogate [W4220703499.c025]. What makes the knowing of Maren's noon act rather than merely correlated with it is that the knowing is of that act as present to God, and nothing in the modal profile separates 'tracking a fact' from 'knowing it' when the fact is present to the knower; the asymmetry concerns the direction of dependence, not the existence of a relation. The objector's test (a state whose content varies with the fact while the state does not depend on it is not yet a knowing) is a further premise, and I concede the argument does not supply a defence of it. The remark that it is a mistake to say anything is logically prior to God's whole act [W4220703499.c038] supports the denial of upstream determination but does not show the knowing is of the act and not of a correlate. So the argument survives only if eternal presence is itself the relation that makes tracking a knowing, and that identification is the premise the argument needs but does not state.

Revised premise: God's knowing of a temporal act is knowledge of that act, rather than a correlated disposition, because the act is eternally present to God, so that presence itself is the answerability relation between knowing and object.

objection.text: Consider an eternal being, Alpha, for whom all times are present. At the eternal now, Jones's choice of cake over pie is fully present. If the duplicate were generated by a glitch while the act failed to occur, Alpha would still register "Jones chooses cake." Thus Alpha's state is merely a correlated disposition toward the duplicate. The actual choice is eternally present, but presence alone does not make Alpha's cognition answerable to the real act; it remains answerable to the internal copy. In the classical framework the argument assumes, God is not a being whose mind hosts a representation distinct from the object; rather, the act's eternal presence just is the knowing. objection.text: Professor Chen posits an eternal God with all time present to Him. This respects divine foreknowledge: God timelessly knows S's choice at T2. It respects libertarian freedom: God's eternal awareness doesn't causally determine S's choice—S deliberates and decides autonomously. Yet reconciliation fails given this very theory of time. If all moments are equally real and present to God, S's future choice at T2 is as fixed as any past event. At T1, S faces no genuinely open alternatives: his choosing A at T2 is an unchangeable feature of the eternal landscape, just as Caesar's crossing the Rubicon is settled. The eternalist theory of time that supports God's timeless knowledge simultaneously eliminates the open future libertarian freedom requires.
